Oliver, this post's search for truth, while interesting, is filled with materialistic undertones which are not just cynical, but also empirically false.

In this post, "reward" is a straight euphemism for money or fame which can be easily converted into money. To that end, the post is completely correct that people are financially compensated based on the number of other people affected by their work, and to the degree of that affect, (i.e. writing a book which someone else reads is compensated less per person than saving a life), rather than by their own supposed sense of the "quality" of their work.

However, the real rewards people have in their lives are not only financial. Experimental research into the effects of money on happiness have consistently found that a financial boon produces a euphoria which is short lived, whether it be getting a raise at work or winning the lottery. Yet when you assume implicitly that Kim Kardashian has been more "rewarded" by society than a good school teacher (as you do in a comment reply), you are completely dismissing non financial rewards in life, some of which are very long lasting and much better at increasing happiness than money. A good teacher will change lives, and will get to see that change in their students as they mature. That has value. Maybe even more value than gracing the cover of Cosmopolitan.

Fair or unfair, for the good of yourself and of your readers, try to remember the goal in life is not in being rich, but in being happy.

I agree to some extent, but it's important to remember that life is not really about winning at every level here. Life is not a competition, some aspects of life are. If you see everything in life as a competition you will think in terms of winning and losing when in reality, life is more of a gray zone than a black-and-white win-lose situation. It's important to remember that even if you see life as a competition, you don't have to win at everything... and that's ok.

Example: The job I had one year ago paid arguably more than what my current job does. My current job makes me work equally much - if not more - but I'm much happier here due to coworkers and bosses being great. According to the article I'm "losing" in terms of wealth. In my view, I don't care as it doesn't matter to me that much.

You have to decide what is important to you and what isn't, and not be upset about someone else having a higher salary, or better love-life or whatever you're currently annoyed about. Personally, collaboration is way more fun than competition even when it comes to things that I'm particularly good at because I'm more interested in a learning experience rather than winning.

Besides, let's assume that you see everything as a competition, and you do your best all your life to 'win' at every aspect. Then what? You die and no one gives a shit about you anymore? Maybe you're remembered by many people, so what? No, I say focus on the things that fulfill and enrich your life instead of working a job you don't like to buy things you don't need to impress people you don't like.
